title: Cryptarithms and symbol-to-digit arithmetic
transcript: In a cryptarithm, a letter stands for one digit wherever it appears. Different letters use different digits when the question says so. Work by place value. A carry is an extra clue linking one column to the next.

An AMC number puzzle may replace digits with letters or boxes. Check whether repeated symbols are required to have the same value. In a Rossmoyne style puzzle, a leading digit or the size of the answer can cut down the possible carries first.
The same digit A is added to itself and the result is six. Which digit is A? Keep both copies of A the same while you solve the number sentence.
The left side is twice the digit A. Dividing the whole result by two keeps the equality balanced. Half of six is three. Substitute the digit in both places to check the original addition.
The two-digit number A five is added to itself. The answer has tens digit seven and units digit B. A and B are distinct digits. Where does the carry come from and what are the two digits?

The units give five plus five, which is ten. Write zero in the units and carry one ten. Now twice A plus one equals seven. Subtract one from the tens total, then halve it. A is three and B is zero. Adding the two finished numbers checks both columns.

A B plus A B gives B C D. All four letters stand for distinct digits. The leading digits A and B are nonzero. Find the smallest such number A B. Use the carry into hundreds before you try possible tens digits.

The largest possible sum of two two-digit numbers is below two hundred, so the hundreds digit B is one. Now the units are one plus one. That gives D equals two, with no carry into the tens. The tens double A and must reach ten. That means A is at least five. Check distinct digits as you choose A.

Start at five. Five gives C equals zero, distinct from the other letters. This endpoint of the possible tens digits already works. So A B is fifty-one. Its double is one hundred and two, with the required repeated digit at the front of the answer.

Treat A B as a two-digit number. A is worth ten times as much in the tens place as it would be in the units. Look for a leading zero and a repeated value assigned to different letters. Check every symbol after the arithmetic works.

Write the columns and mark the possible carries. Use the very first digit of a three-digit sum to narrow your options. After solving, put each value back into the original expression. An equality and a legal assignment are both required.
